---
title: "Example: Google translation of a multilingual corpus"
output: html_document
params:
  live: false
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
run_live <- isTRUE(params$live)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE, error = FALSE)
library(quallmer)
library(quanteda)
if (run_live) {
  if (!nzchar(Sys.getenv("GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT"))) {
    stop("Set GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT before rendering the live article.")
  }
} else {
  google_translated <- readRDS("data/translated_udhr_google.rds")
  udhr <- inputs(google_translated)
  udhr_ids <- names(google_translated)
  recorded_date <- format(
    attr(google_translated, "provenance")$timestamp[1],
    "%d %B %Y", tz = "UTC"
  )
}
```

Google's specialised [Translation LLM](https://docs.cloud.google.com/translate/docs/translation-llm)
can translate a multilingual corpus into a common language using
`qlm_translate()`. This example translates six complete versions of the Universal
Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) into British English, retains the source texts
and translation records, and converts the result back to a quanteda corpus.

`r if (run_live) "This page executes a fresh Google API run." else paste0("The output below comes from a saved Google API run on **", recorded_date, "**.")`
Routine site builds load the saved results and execute the inspection, corpus
conversion and validation code without making API calls. Project identifiers in
the published fixture have been replaced with placeholders; source texts,
translations and their hashes are unchanged. Live mode reruns the six-document
translation against Google. Installation and credential setup remain manual.
Live translation requests are billed to your Google Cloud project.

## Set up Google Cloud

Follow Google's [Cloud Translation setup guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/translate/docs/setup).
You need a project with billing enabled, the Cloud Translation API enabled, and
an API key that permits access to that API.

1. Create or select a project in the [Google Cloud console](https://console.cloud.google.com/).
   Record its **project ID**, which can differ from its display name.
2. Under **APIs & Services → Library**, find **Cloud Translation API** and enable it.
3. Under **APIs & Services → Credentials**, create an API key. Give it a name
   such as **Translation**, and restrict its allowed APIs to **Cloud Translation API**.
4. Copy the key using **Show key** in the Credentials list.

Enabling the API for a project and allowing a key to call it are separate settings.
A key restricted to Gemini does not authorise Cloud Translation. A dedicated
translation key makes the intended access clear.

Quallmer's model identifier is `"google-translate/translation-llm"`. It selects
Google's standard `general/translation-llm` model through the Cloud Translation
Basic API, which accepts API-key authentication.

## Save credentials

### Use the system keyring

Save the API key once with the optional keyring package:

```{r save-key, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("keyring") # once, if needed
keyring::key_set("google-translate")
```

Paste the API key at the password prompt. A successful save normally produces no
printed output. On macOS, the key is stored in Keychain; access may prompt you to
unlock or permit access to the entry. No `.Renviron` entry is needed for this key.

Set the project separately. The project ID is configuration, not a secret:

```{r project, eval=FALSE}
library(quallmer)
Sys.setenv(GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT = "your-project-id")
```

### Use environment variables

The default key variable is **`GOOGLE_TRANSLATE_API_KEY`**. If you prefer
environment variables, these lines can go in your home `~/.Renviron`:

```text
GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=your-project-id
GOOGLE_TRANSLATE_API_KEY=your-api-key
```

Replace the placeholders and restart R. This file stores the key as plain text;
keep it outside version control. `.Renviron` contains assignments, so do not put
`keyring::key_get()` calls in it. R started with `--vanilla` does not read this file.

Credential precedence is:

| Source | How it is supplied |
|:--|:--|
| Explicit key | `api_key = ...` in `qlm_translate()` |
| Environment | `GOOGLE_TRANSLATE_API_KEY` |
| Optional keyring fallback | `keyring::key_get("google-translate")` |

An environment variable takes precedence over the keyring entry. If it contains
an old key, remove or update it before testing a newly saved key. Quallmer does
not copy retrieved keys into the environment or translation provenance.

An explicit argument also lets you use your own environment-variable name:

```{r explicit-key, eval=FALSE}
greeting <- qlm_translate(
  c(fr = "Bonjour, comment allez-vous ?"),
  model = "google-translate/translation-llm",
  to = "en-GB",
  project_id = "your-project-id",
  api_key = Sys.getenv("MY_TRANSLATION_KEY")
)
```

## Check access with a short vector

Before sending full documents, translate two short texts. This call uses the
project environment variable and resolves the API key automatically:

```{r greeting, eval=FALSE}
greetings <- qlm_translate(
  c(fr = "Bonjour tout le monde.", de = "Guten Morgen."),
  model = "google-translate/translation-llm",
  to = "en-GB"
)
greetings
```

The result is a `qlm_translation`: a character vector of translations named
after the inputs, with `NA` for any failure. `attr(greetings, "provenance")`
holds the record of each translation, including the reason for a failure.
`as.character(greetings)` drops that record.

## Select six complete UDHR documents

The [quanteda.corpora package](https://github.com/quanteda/quanteda.corpora)
contains `data_corpus_udhr`, a collection of UDHR texts in many languages.
Install the example packages if needed:

```{r install-data, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(c("quanteda", "remotes"))
remotes::install_github("quanteda/quanteda.corpora")
```

Load quanteda before subsetting the corpus, then select German, French, Spanish,
Simplified Chinese, Hindi and Russian. These are complete documents, including
their headings and preambles:

```{r select-udhr, eval=run_live}
library(quanteda)

udhr_ids <- c("deu_1996", "fra", "spa", "cmn_hans", "hin", "rus")
udhr <- quanteda.corpora::data_corpus_udhr[udhr_ids]
```

```{r udhr-inventory}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  .id = docnames(udhr),
  language = docvars(udhr)$Name,
  characters = unname(nchar(as.character(udhr)))
), row.names = FALSE)
```

The source corpus also has four document variables: `Key`, `Name`, `ISO` and
`Direction`. They describe the original documents and remain available after
translation.

## Translate the corpus into English

Omit `from` to let Google detect each document's language independently:

```{r translate-udhr, eval=run_live}
google_timing <- system.time(
  google_translated <- qlm_translate(
    udhr,
    model = "google-translate/translation-llm",
    to = "en-GB",
    on_error = "continue"
  )
)

google_timing
google_translated
```

```{r saved-translation-output, echo=FALSE, eval=!run_live}
google_translated
```

Each of these documents fits in a single request. The adapter sends one document
per request, defaulting to two concurrent requests and pacing submissions
according to `rpm`. It splits a larger document only when needed to fit its
30,000-character or 100 kB JSON-body limit, or when you request a smaller
`chunk_size`. See Google's [quotas and limits](https://docs.cloud.google.com/translate/quotas).
Google handles paragraph formatting; exact original blank-line separators are
not guaranteed.

`from` is a call-wide setting. For a homogeneous selection you can supply,
for example, `from = "fr"`; automatic source-language detection is then
not performed. Leave it unset for this six-language selection.

The model location defaults to `region = "us-central1"`; pass another as
`qlm_translate(..., region = "europe-west4")`. You can also supply
`project_id` directly instead of setting `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT`. The Basic API
uses a global endpoint, so the model location alone does not guarantee where
data is processed. See Google's [data usage FAQ](https://docs.cloud.google.com/translate/data-usage).

## Inspect translations and provenance

The original corpus is retained separately from the translated output:

```{r inspect-results}
identical(inputs(google_translated), udhr)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  .id = names(google_translated),
  excerpt = substr(as.character(google_translated), 1, 120)
), row.names = FALSE)

google_provenance <- attr(google_translated, "provenance")
knitr::kable(google_provenance[c(
  ".id", "status", "detected_language", ".error", "reported_model"
)], row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r check-translations, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  inherits(google_translated, "qlm_translation"),
  identical(names(google_translated), udhr_ids),
  identical(inputs(google_translated), udhr),
  all(google_provenance$status == "ok"),
  !anyNA(google_translated),
  all(nzchar(google_translated)),
  identical(google_provenance$output_hash, vapply(as.character(google_translated),
    function(text) digest::digest(enc2utf8(text), algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE),
    "", USE.NAMES = FALSE)),
  identical(google_provenance$source_hash, vapply(as.character(udhr),
    function(text) digest::digest(enc2utf8(text), algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE),
    "", USE.NAMES = FALSE)),
  identical(google_provenance$detected_language, c("de", "fr", "es", "zh", "hi", "ru")),
  all(grepl("translation-llm", google_provenance$reported_model, fixed = TRUE))
)
```

These language detections come from the recorded responses; subsequent API
responses can differ. The `ISO`
docvar uses the original corpus's three-letter codes, whereas Google returned
the codes above. Both are retained. Translation provenance also records the
source text, source and output hashes, requested model and settings, and attempts.
Detected language is Google's assessment of the supplied document; it is not a
language label for the translated output, whose requested language is `en-GB`.

For bilingual review, place original and translated texts side by side:

```{r bilingual-review}
review <- data.frame(
  .id = names(google_translated),
  source = unname(as.character(inputs(google_translated))),
  translation = unname(as.character(google_translated))
)
review_preview <- review
review_preview[c("source", "translation")] <- lapply(
  review_preview[c("source", "translation")], substr, start = 1, stop = 150
)
knitr::kable(review_preview[review_preview$.id == "hin", ], row.names = FALSE)

results_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "udhr-google-english.rds")
saveRDS(google_translated, results_file)
```

Saving the result retains the exact translated texts and provenance for reuse;
rerunning a model alias later may produce different wording. This example writes
to a temporary directory; choose a permanent path when saving it for analysis.

## Convert back to a corpus

Convert the translations with quanteda's `corpus()`:

```{r corpus-conversion}
google_corpus <- quanteda::corpus(google_translated)

docnames(google_corpus)
docvars(google_corpus)
identical(docvars(google_corpus), docvars(udhr))
identical(meta(google_corpus, type = "system"), meta(udhr, type = "system"))

meta(google_corpus, "quallmer")$translation[c(".id", "status", "detected_language")]
```

```{r check-corpus, include=FALSE}
original_user <- meta(udhr, type = "user")
restored_user <- meta(google_corpus, type = "user")
restored_user$quallmer <- NULL
stopifnot(
  identical(docnames(google_corpus), udhr_ids),
  identical(docvars(google_corpus), docvars(udhr)),
  identical(meta(google_corpus, type = "system"), meta(udhr, type = "system")),
  identical(restored_user, original_user),
  identical(meta(google_corpus, "quallmer")$translation, google_provenance)
)
```

The corpus contains the English translations, with the same document names and
original document variables. Its original system and user metadata are restored;
text summary caches are cleared. The `quallmer` user-metadata field holds the
translation provenance.

You can then use ordinary quanteda operations. For example, the source-language
docvar identifies the translation made from Hindi:

```{r use-corpus}
hindi_english <- corpus_subset(google_corpus, ISO == "hin")
cat(substr(as.character(hindi_english)[[1]], 1, 400), "\n")

google_tokens <- tokens(google_corpus, remove_punct = TRUE)
ntoken(google_tokens)
```

```{r check-tokens, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  all(ntoken(google_tokens) > 0L),
  identical(docvars(google_tokens), docvars(udhr))
)
```

Quanteda is optional for `qlm_translate()` itself; it is used here to load,
subset and analyse the example corpus. A named character vector works without
it, as the greeting example illustrates. Text outputs of `qlm_code()` can also
be converted, using `quanteda::corpus(coded, text_field = "summary")`.

## Inspect failures and retry selected documents

With `on_error = "continue"`, successful translations remain available when
another request fails. A failed or unsubmitted document is `NA`. Inspect the
recorded errors before retrying:

```{r retry-failures, eval=FALSE}
google_provenance[google_provenance$status != "ok", c(".id", "status", ".error")]

failed <- is.na(google_translated)
if (any(failed)) {
  retried <- qlm_translate(
    inputs(google_translated)[failed],
    model = "google-translate/translation-llm",
    to = "en-GB",
    on_error = "continue"
  )
  google_translated[failed] <- retried
}
```

For a **403 Forbidden** response, check both API enablement and the key's API
restrictions in the project that owns the key. Also check that you are using its
project ID and have billing enabled. If the key was recently changed, allow time
for its restrictions to take effect. Google documents the blocked-service error
in its [authentication troubleshooting guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/troubleshoot-auth-manager#api-key-service-blocked).

This adapter exposes the standard Translation LLM through the Basic API. It
rejects `context`, `instructions`, `glossary` and non-empty `params`
because these options are not supported on this route. The result records the
model Google reports; it does not pin a permanent model version.

The translations can be passed directly to `qlm_code()`, which records
translation as a preprocessing stage. See
[Translating before coding](example_translation.html) for that workflow.

## Run this article as a live check

Routine builds check the saved output, its hashes and the conversion workflow.
They do not establish that current credentials or Google's service work. Unit tests mock responses to check request construction,
error handling and metadata preservation. Live verification executes this article's
actual UDHR chunks against Google, checks all six results, source-language
detections, retained inputs, restored corpus metadata and tokenization, and
produces an HTML page containing the real output. These checks establish that the
workflow ran successfully; bilingual review is still needed to assess fidelity.

From a local checkout of quallmer, after installing the example packages and
saving your key, run:

```{r live-check, eval=FALSE}
Sys.setenv(GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT = "your-project-id")
source("dev/translation-google-udhr-live-check.R")
```

The script loads the checkout, renders with `params = list(live = TRUE)`, retains
`google_translated`, `google_provenance` and `google_corpus` in your session, and
saves the translated object and rendered page in a temporary results directory.
It prints their paths and stops with an error if an assertion fails. It does not
install packages, save credentials or automatically run the retry example.

You can also render the article directly after loading the package:

```{r live-render, eval=FALSE}
rmarkdown::render(
  "vignettes/pkgdown/examples/example_translation_google.Rmd",
  params = list(live = TRUE),
  output_dir = tempdir()
)
```

To replace the published fixture after reviewing a fresh live run, enable the
refresh option before running the script:

```{r refresh-saved-results, eval=FALSE}
options(quallmer.update_google_article_cache = TRUE)
source("dev/translation-google-udhr-live-check.R")
options(quallmer.update_google_article_cache = NULL)
```

This explicitly updates `data/translated_udhr_google.rds` beside the article,
using the new real results with project identifiers replaced by placeholders.
Normal site builds only read this fixture.
